title: Platform work in Geneva: the second discussion in June 2026
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What the ILO's June 2026 platform-economy discussion was about, what India's Code on Social Security already says, and an update on the convention adopted on 12 June.
body:
In June 2026 the **114th session of the International Labour Conference** meets in Geneva. One item dominates the workers' agenda: **decent work in the platform economy**. After a first discussion in 2025, the item returns for a second and final discussion, at which the Conference is expected to decide what form of international standard to adopt: a **convention**, a **recommendation**, or both. For a country like India, with a very large and fast-growing platform workforce, the outcome matters directly. This post explains how the International Labour Organization (ILO) makes standards, what the open questions are, what India's own law already says, and how to follow the proceedings. An update at the end records what happened once the Conference had met.

## How the ILO makes a standard

The ILO is unusual among international bodies because each member country sends a **tripartite delegation**: two representatives of the Government, one of employers and one of workers. All four have the right to speak and vote individually, which means that the workers' and employers' delegates are not bound by the Government's position. A standard-setting item normally goes through a **double discussion**. In the first year the Conference debates a report and decides whether to proceed and in what form; in the second year it works on a draft text prepared from that discussion. A convention, once adopted by the Conference, does not bind any country until the country ratifies it. A recommendation is guidance only and is not open to ratification. That difference is why the choice between the two is the most closely watched question in Geneva.

## Points of contention

The platform-economy discussion has turned on a handful of difficult issues.

- **Who is covered.** Should the standard apply to all platform workers, including those who do online tasks such as data labelling, or only to certain kinds of in-person work such as taxi driving and delivery? Governments also differ on whether they may exclude some categories.
- **Employment status.** Workers' representatives want the standard to make it harder for a platform to label a worker as an independent contractor when the real relationship looks like employment. Employers prefer flexibility. Some propose a binary of employee and self-employed; others favour recognising a new category with its own set of rights.
- **Algorithmic management.** Platforms use software to assign work, set prices, rate performance and sometimes deactivate accounts. The question is how much transparency workers can demand, and whether a human being must review serious decisions such as suspension or deactivation.
- **Social protection.** Who pays for accident cover, health care, maternity benefit and pension for people who work through several platforms and have no single employer?
- **Collective bargaining.** How can workers who are scattered, work alone and are classed as self-employed organise and negotiate? Competition law in some countries treats collective bargaining by the self-employed as a restriction on trade.

## What India's law already says

India does not come to Geneva with a blank slate. The **Code on Social Security, 2020**, one of the four labour codes brought into effect from 21 November 2025, is the Indian law that defines **gig workers** and **platform workers**. A gig worker is a person who earns from work outside a traditional employer-employee relationship; platform work is such work where an online platform connects people to solve problems or provide services for payment. The Central Government can notify other activities as platform work.

The Code also creates an **aggregator contribution**. According to a Government backgrounder, aggregators, meaning the digital intermediaries that connect users with service providers, must contribute between 1 and 2 per cent of their annual turnover to a Social Security Fund, subject to a cap of 5 per cent of the amounts paid or payable to gig and platform workers. The Fund can also draw on government sources and other contributions. Workers can register themselves on the **e-Shram** portal, which issues an Aadhaar-linked identity that keeps benefits portable when a worker moves between platforms. Registered workers become eligible for notified benefits such as accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, and the Government may set up a helpline or facilitation centre for grievances.

Commentators have noted what the Code does not do. It treats gig and platform workers as separate categories and does not classify them as employees, and it has no test equivalent to the idea, now common in international discussion, that the facts of how work is done should decide status regardless of the label in the contract. Those gaps are the reason the ILO text is of such interest in India.

## India's tripartite delegation and BMS

India's delegation consists of Government, employer and worker representatives, who must reach their own positions. BMS is part of the workers' side and has a representative in the delegation. Its general line on the subject, as stated at the Conference, is that technology must serve human beings and that fair treatment should extend to platform workers.

## How to follow the proceedings

The ILO publishes daily bulletins and the Conference's record of proceedings online, and the final texts appear on the ILO website under the Conference documents. Readers should rely on those documents and on official summaries rather than on social-media paraphrase, because the precise words, such as whether a provision says "shall" or "should consider", decide what a standard actually requires.

## Update after the Conference

The Conference ran from 1 to 12 June 2026 and closed with a historic result. It adopted the **Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy, 2026**, numbered **Convention No. 193**, the first international labour standard aimed at digital labour platforms. The vote, as reported by Human Rights Watch, was 406 in favour, 8 against and 36 abstentions. The convention covers all digital labour platforms and requires member States to ensure that platform workers enjoy basic rights at work, including freedom of association and collective bargaining, protection from discrimination and a safe and healthy working environment, whatever their status under national law. It also deals with the correct classification of workers based mainly on how the work is actually performed, with transparency in automated decision-making, with a right to a written explanation and meaningful human review of serious adverse decisions, and with access to social security on terms no less favourable than for other workers of the same status. A separate, more detailed recommendation was not finalised for lack of time.

India's delegation did not speak with one voice. According to a LiveLaw commentary, the Government delegate abstained while the employers' and workers' delegates voted in favour. India has given no official explanation for the abstention, and ratification of the convention is therefore not imminent. Speaking in Geneva on 9 June, BMS's representative told the Conference that fair treatment should extend to gig and platform workers and welcomed the social security steps taken by India and some States. BMS will return to the outcome and its implications for India in a later post.
